To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the influenza virus matrix protein M 1 forms large clusters with a layered architecture in solution at acidic pH.
the M1 protein is anisotropic, flexible and self-assembles into ordered supramolecular structures.
the M1 matrix protein of the influenza A virus is structurally anisometric with the C-terminal domain being flexible and the N-terminal domain being rigid.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the structural organisation of the matrix protein M1 and its self-assemblies, which is important for the viral replication cycle.
the structural organisation of influenza A virus matrix protein in solution and at the lipid-like surface.
the structural analysis of the M1 matrix protein from influenza virus and its self-assembly at low pH.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the structural organisation of influenza virus M1 is a dynamic process that is dependent on the local environment and the surrounding proteins.
the M1 C-terminus plays a crucial role in the self-assembly of M1, which is a prerequisite for the formation of the virus particle.
the C-terminal domain is the key structural component of M1, which is responsible for its self-assembly and the structural organisation of the influenza viral membrane.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we provide the first structural analysis of full-length M1 and its supramolecular assemblies at acidic pH.

we have shown the importance of the C-terminal domain of M1 for the formation of large clusters in acidic solution and the importance of the NM-domain in the formation of virion-like structures in the presence of lipid bilayer.
we have provided a structural basis for a more detailed understanding of the role of M1 in viral replication and assembly.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the M1 structure and its self-assembly at low pH is a dynamic process that is driven by the pH-dependent conformational changes in the C-terminal domain of the protein.
the M1 self-assembly process can be controlled by the pH of the solution.

the M1 C-terminal tail is a flexible, but not completely unstructured, polypeptide that is responsible for the formation of supranucleocapsid-like structures in solution and the formation of the layered architecture of the viral membrane.
